spec_section_focus: Wider world depth study, peacemaking through to the outbreak of war

teaching_brief.scope: From the November 1918 armistice through the Paris peacemaking, the rise and collapse of the League of Nations, and the diplomatic road to the German invasion of Poland in September 1939. Students study the complex and diverse interests of states and individuals — including Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George, Stresemann, Hitler, Mussolini, Stalin and Chamberlain — and concepts of national self-determination, internationalism and treaty revision.

examiner_signals.signal: Source-utility (12 marks) responses must integrate content, provenance AND the student's own contextual knowledge — answers that handle only two of the three are capped below the top band.
examiner_signals.source: AQA examiner report guidance on Paper 1 Section B source-utility questions; AQA-81451BB-EX answers and commentaries

examiner_signals.signal: Narrative accounts (8 marks) reward causal links between events ('this then triggered…' / 'because of this…'), not chronological listing. Top-band answers analyse the sequence as a chain of causes and consequences.
examiner_signals.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

examiner_signals.signal: Source-based essay (16 marks) answers do not need a formal introduction or conclusion to reach full marks — examiners advise students begin evaluating sources directly. Each source must receive a substantiated judgement on utility.
examiner_signals.source: AQA Notes and Guidance for Paper 1 Section B; published examiner commentary

examiner_signals.signal: Substantiated overall judgement on the source-based essay must address the question's specific claim — generic 'sources are useful in different ways' conclusions do not reach the top band.
examiner_signals.source: AQA principal examiner commentary on 16-mark source-based essay performance

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students assume the Treaty of Versailles was uniquely punitive. In fact the terms imposed by Germany on Russia at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 were significantly harsher in territorial scale, and the Versailles terms reflected a compromise between Wilson's Fourteen Points and French security demands.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today archive on the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk; AQA examiner commentary on candidates' over-reliance on the 'Diktat' framing

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students confuse the Council (great powers, permanent members, decisions) with the Assembly (all members, one vote each, debate forum) and miss that decisions required unanimity, which crippled responses to the Manchurian and Abyssinian crises.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today, 'The League of Nations: A League of its Own' (Henig)

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students frame appeasement as moral failure or cowardice. Modern historians stress it was a rational policy given Britain's overstretched empire, public pacifism after 1918, military weakness in 1938, lack of allies (USA isolationist, USSR distrusted) and Chamberlain's sincere belief that another war was avoidable.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today, McDonough on Chamberlain; 'Chamberlain — Guilty Man or National Saviour?'

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students conflate the September 1938 Munich Agreement (transferring the Sudetenland), the German military occupation of the Sudetenland in October 1938, and Hitler's seizure of the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. Each is a distinct event with distinct international reactions, and only the March 1939 occupation ended British appeasement.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today, 'The Munich Conference'; AQA examiner reports flagging chronological confusion in narrative accounts

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students treat the Manchurian (1931) and Abyssinian (1935-36) crises as the same kind of failure. They differ critically: in Manchuria the League had little leverage and Japan resigned; in Abyssinia the League imposed sanctions but excluded oil and let Britain and France negotiate the secret Hoare-Laval Pact, destroying its credibility.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today archive on the League's collapse; Henig on League failures

common_misconceptions_unit.misconception: Students present Hitler's 1933-39 foreign policy as a master plan executed step by step. A.J.P. Taylor's controversial 'Origins of the Second World War' (1961) argued Hitler was an opportunist exploiting circumstances, and modern historians sit between intentionalist and structuralist positions — examiners reward nuance over a single causal narrative.
common_misconceptions_unit.source: History Today archive review essays on Taylor and the appeasement debate

teaching_brief.tier_split: No Foundation/Higher tier in AQA GCSE History 8145 — single-tier paper. Do not flag content as higher_only.
teaching_brief.spec_changes_2026: No subject-content changes for the 2026 series. Spec remains 24 September 2019 v1.3.
teaching_brief.historiography_notes: Use sparingly and only where AQA examiner reports flag candidate misconceptions. Two debates are relevant: (1) Taylor's intentionalist-vs-opportunist reading of Hitler — useful for the responsibility-for-war essay; (2) the 'Guilty Men' (Cato, 1940) vs revisionist (Reynolds, McDonough) debate on appeasement. Both should be presented as competing interpretations rather than settled answers.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Woodrow Wilson
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US President; Fourteen Points; pushed self-determination and the League

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Georges Clemenceau
key_individuals_and_groups.role: French PM; demanded reparations and security against Germany

key_individuals_and_groups.name: David Lloyd George
key_individuals_and_groups.role: British PM; sought a middle ground between Wilson and Clemenceau

key_individuals_and_groups.role: Italian PM; left Versailles dissatisfied over territorial promises

key_individuals_and_groups.role: German Foreign Minister; reconciliation policy, Locarno, League entry

lessons.title: The Armistice and the Aims of the Peacemakers
lessons.description: How November 1918 ended the fighting and what Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George each wanted from peace.
spec_bullets_covered: The armistice: aims of the peacemakers; Wilson and the Fourteen Points; Clemenceau and Lloyd George; the extent to which they achieved their aims.
lessons.narrative_arc: Set up the conditions in which peacemaking happened: a Germany that had not been invaded, an exhausted France, a war-weary Britain, and an idealistic America arriving late. Use the contrast in aims to frame the rest of the unit.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 2 (Versailles terms reflect compromise between these aims)

lessons.title: The Versailles Settlement: Terms and Diktat
lessons.description: The five sections of the Treaty: territorial losses, military restrictions, war guilt and reparations.
spec_bullets_covered: The Versailles Settlement: Diktat; territorial changes; military restrictions; war guilt and reparations.
key_dates_or_events: 28 June 1919 signing of Treaty of Versailles
Loss of Alsace-Lorraine, Saar, Posen, Danzig, all colonies
Army cap 100,000; no air force; Rhineland demilitarised; £6.6bn reparations
lessons.narrative_arc: Walk through what Germany lost in clear blocks (territory, military, money, blame), then frame why each was demanded by which peacemaker. End by contrasting Versailles with the harsher Brest-Litovsk terms Germany had imposed on Russia.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 9 (Hitler's revision of these terms drives the 1930s crisis)

lessons.title: Reactions to the Treaty and the Wider Settlement
lessons.description: Allied disagreements, German fury and the strengths and weaknesses of the wider settlement.
spec_bullets_covered: Impact of the treaty and wider settlement: reactions of the Allies; German objections; strengths and weaknesses of the settlement, including the problems faced by new states.
key_dates_or_events: 1919-20 treaties of Saint-Germain, Trianon, Neuilly, Sèvres
1920 US Senate rejection of Treaty and League
lessons.narrative_arc: Three audiences: the Allies (each disappointed for different reasons — Wilson's Senate rejected the League; Italy felt cheated; France thought Germany got off lightly); Germany (Diktat, war guilt, military emasculation); the new states (small, ethnically mixed, bordered by resentful neighbours). End with a balanced judgement on whether the settlement was workable.

lessons.title: The League of Nations: Structure and Membership
lessons.description: How the League was formed, its Council, Assembly, agencies and the great powers that joined or stayed out.
spec_bullets_covered: The League of Nations: its formation and covenant; organisation; membership and how it changed; the powers of the League.
key_concepts: moral condemnation, economic sanctions, military force
lessons.narrative_arc: Build the League as a machine: Council (great powers, permanent + non-permanent), Assembly (all members), Secretariat, Court, ILO. Stress the absence of USA, Germany (until 1926) and USSR (until 1934), and the unanimity requirement that would later paralyse decision-making.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 1 (Wilson's Fourteen Points seeded the idea)
Lesson 5 (1920s case studies test these mechanisms)
Lesson 7 (1930s crises expose the structural weaknesses)

lessons.title: The League's 1920s Record: Successes and Failures
lessons.description: Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia, Vilna, Corfu and Bulgaria — where the League worked and where it didn't.
spec_bullets_covered: The work of the League's agencies; the contribution of the League to peace in the 1920s, including the successes and failures of the League, such as the Aaland Islands, Upper Silesia, Vilna, Corfu and Bulgaria.
lessons.narrative_arc: Pair successes (Aaland, Bulgaria, Upper Silesia and humanitarian work) against failures (Vilna, Corfu) to show the League could resolve disputes between small states but folded when a great power was the aggressor — foreshadowing the 1930s.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 4 (structure determines what the League could and couldn't do)
Lesson 7 (Manchuria and Abyssinia confirm the great-power problem)

lessons.title: Diplomacy Outside the League: Locarno and Kellogg-Briand
lessons.description: Stresemann's reconciliation, the 1925 Locarno treaties and the 1928 pact that renounced war.
spec_bullets_covered: Diplomacy outside the League: Locarno treaties and the Kellogg-Briand Pact.
lessons.narrative_arc: Show the late 1920s as a high-water mark of internationalism — Germany rehabilitated, western borders guaranteed, war 'outlawed'. End by flagging that Locarno guaranteed only Germany's western borders, leaving Poland and Czechoslovakia exposed.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 7 (the spirit collapses with the Depression)

lessons.title: The Collapse of the League: Manchuria and Abyssinia
lessons.description: How the Depression and two great-power aggressions destroyed the League's credibility.
spec_bullets_covered: The collapse of the League: the effects of the Depression; the Manchurian and Abyssinian crises and their consequences; the failure of the League to avert war in 1939.
lessons.narrative_arc: Three blows: (1) the Depression undermined collective economic action; (2) Manchuria showed sanctions were toothless against a determined great power on a distant continent; (3) Abyssinia destroyed the League's moral authority when Britain and France were exposed plotting to give Mussolini what he wanted. By 1936 the League had failed as a deterrent.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 10 (Hitler reads the lesson and remilitarises the Rhineland)

lessons.title: Hitler's Aims and Early Foreign Policy 1933-1934
lessons.description: Hitler's foreign-policy aims, the Dollfuss Affair and the first Allied reactions.
spec_bullets_covered: The development of tension: Hitler's aims and Allied reactions; the Dollfuss Affair.
key_dates_or_events: October 1933 Germany leaves League and Disarmament Conference
July 1934 Dollfuss assassinated; Mussolini moves troops to Brenner Pass
lessons.narrative_arc: Set out Hitler's three intertwined aims (revise Versailles, unite German speakers, win Lebensraum in the east), then show 1933-34 as a cautious testing phase — withdrawal from the League went unpunished, but the Austrian coup attempt was checked by Mussolini, not by Britain or France.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 3 (Versailles is the target of revision)
Lesson 9 (Saar, rearmament, Stresa Front escalate the challenge)

lessons.title: The Saar, Rearmament and the Stresa Front 1935
lessons.description: The Saar plebiscite, open conscription, the short-lived Stresa Front and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement.
spec_bullets_covered: The Saar; German rearmament, including conscription; the Stresa Front; Anglo-German Naval Agreement.
key_dates_or_events: January 1935 Saar plebiscite (90% to return to Germany)
March 1935 Hitler announces conscription and Luftwaffe
October 1935 Italy invades Abyssinia, Stresa collapses
lessons.narrative_arc: 1935 as the pivot year: a legitimate plebiscite handed Hitler the Saar; he then openly broke Versailles by announcing conscription; Britain, France and Italy briefly aligned at Stresa to oppose German revision; but Britain undercut the front within weeks by signing a separate naval deal — a textbook example of how the Allies failed to maintain a united response.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 10 (Rhineland follows the breakdown of allied unity)

lessons.title: Escalation: Rhineland, Axis and Anti-Comintern
lessons.description: The 1936 remilitarisation of the Rhineland, the Rome-Berlin Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
spec_bullets_covered: Escalation of tension: remilitarisation of the Rhineland; Mussolini, the Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
lessons.narrative_arc: The Rhineland as the decisive turning point: Hitler defied Versailles AND Locarno with a small force that had orders to retreat if challenged. France did not act, Britain shrugged ('they're only going into their own back garden'). Once Hitler had got away with that, alignment with Mussolini and Japan turned the diplomatic balance further.

lessons.title: Anschluss and the Reasons for Appeasement
lessons.description: The 1938 union with Austria and why Britain chose appeasement as its main response.
spec_bullets_covered: Anschluss; reasons for and against the policy of appeasement.
lessons.narrative_arc: Open with Anschluss as the moment Hitler annexed a sovereign state without a shot fired and without allied response. Then explain why Chamberlain chose appeasement: military weakness in 1938, an empire stretched from Singapore to the Atlantic, the painful memory of 1914-18, distrust of Stalin, isolationist USA, and the sincere belief that grievances could be negotiated. End by flagging the historiographical split between 'Guilty Men' (Cato 1940) and the rational-policy revisionists (McDonough, Reynolds).

lessons.title: The Sudeten Crisis and Munich
lessons.description: Henlein's agitation, the September 1938 crisis, the Munich Agreement and Chamberlain's 'peace for our time'.
key_dates_or_events: 1 October German troops enter the Sudetenland
lessons.narrative_arc: Track the September shuttle diplomacy day by day: Berchtesgaden, Bad Godesberg, Munich. Stress that Czechoslovakia was not at the table, that the Sudetenland contained the country's defensive fortifications, and that Chamberlain returned with the famous paper believing he had bought lasting peace.

lessons.title: The End of Appeasement: Prague and the Polish Guarantee
lessons.description: How the March 1939 occupation of Czechoslovakia and the Polish guarantee changed British policy.
spec_bullets_covered: The ending of appeasement; the occupation of Czechoslovakia.
lessons.narrative_arc: The hinge moment: Hitler's seizure of the rump Czech lands could not be defended by 'self-determination' since the population was not German. British opinion turned, Chamberlain shifted to deterrence with the Polish guarantee, and France followed. Appeasement was over.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 14 (Poland and the outbreak of war)

lessons.title: Nazi-Soviet Pact, Poland and the Outbreak of War
lessons.description: The August 1939 pact, the September invasion of Poland and the responsibility of Hitler, Stalin and Chamberlain.
spec_bullets_covered: The role of the USSR and the Nazi-Soviet Pact; the invasion of Poland and outbreak of war, September 1939; responsibility for the outbreak of war, including that of key individuals: Hitler, Stalin and Chamberlain.
key_dates_or_events: 3 September 1939 Britain and France declare war
17 September 1939 Soviet invasion of eastern Poland
lessons.narrative_arc: Bring the threads together. The pact stunned the world, secured Hitler's eastern flank and dismembered Poland in advance. The September invasion forced the Polish-guarantee promise into action. End with a balanced judgement on responsibility — Hitler as the prime mover, Stalin as opportunist, Chamberlain as the defender of a policy that had finally run out — explicitly flagging Taylor's controversial intentionalist vs opportunist debate.
links_to_other_lessons: Lesson 1 (the war Versailles was meant to make impossible)

spec_coverage_check.notes: Every spec bullet from lines 877-920 is covered. The collapse-of-League bullet ('failure to avert war in 1939') is picked up across L7, L13 and L14 because it is a thread, not a single event.
